prompt: A page control can only be operated by clicking it with a mouse. Who is prevented from using it?
optionA: Anyone using a screen reader only
optionB: Anyone navigating by keyboard
optionC: Anyone with a small screen
optionD: Anyone on a slow connection
correctAnswerText: Anyone navigating by keyboard
explanation: The barrier is about how the control is operated rather than how it is perceived. People navigate by keyboard for many reasons, including motor difficulties and simple preference.

prompt: A status is shown only by making a row red or green. Who is prevented from reading it?
optionA: Anyone navigating by keyboard
optionB: Anyone using a large screen
optionC: Nobody; colour is universally understood
optionD: Anyone who cannot distinguish those colours, and anyone hearing the page read aloud
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot distinguish those colours, and anyone hearing the page read aloud
explanation: Two separate groups are affected by the same fault. Colour vision and non-visual reading are different situations with the same consequence here.

prompt: An image conveys information and carries no description. Who is prevented from getting that information?
optionA: Anyone who cannot see the image
optionB: Anyone navigating by keyboard
optionC: Anyone who cannot distinguish colours
optionD: Anyone using an old browser
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot see the image
explanation: A missing description affects people who do not receive the image itself. Keyboard use and colour vision are unrelated to it.

prompt: What identifies something as an accessibility barrier?
optionA: That the page looks unpolished
optionB: That the page is slow to load
optionC: That a described person cannot do or learn something others can
optionD: That the page has not been tested
correctAnswerText: That a described person cannot do or learn something others can
explanation: A barrier is stated as who is prevented from what. Whether a page looks acceptable is a separate judgement entirely.

prompt: A team fixes every missing image description and declares the page accessible. What is wrong with the conclusion?
optionA: Nothing; image descriptions are the whole of accessibility
optionB: One barrier has been removed and others — keyboard reach, focus order, colour alone — were never examined
optionC: The descriptions should have been checked by a specialist
optionD: The page cannot be accessible until it is retested for speed
correctAnswerText: One barrier has been removed and others — keyboard reach, focus order, colour alone — were never examined
explanation: Image descriptions address people who cannot see images and nobody else. A page can have perfect descriptions and be entirely unusable by keyboard.

prompt: A chart shows the sales figures being discussed, and the figures appear nowhere else on the page. Should it be described?
optionA: No; charts are decorative
optionB: No; the surrounding text is enough
optionC: Only if the page has no other images
optionD: Yes; it carries information available nowhere else
correctAnswerText: Yes; it carries information available nowhere else
explanation: The chart is the only source of those figures, so a reader who cannot see it loses them. That is what makes an image meaningful rather than decorative.

prompt: A decorative swirl separates two sections and carries no information. Should it be described?
optionA: No; it should be passed over silently
optionB: Yes; every image should be described
optionC: Yes; it should be described as a swirl
optionD: Yes; it should be described as decorative
correctAnswerText: No; it should be passed over silently
explanation: Describing it inserts noise into the reading of the page. Being passed over is the correct treatment for an image that says nothing.

prompt: What decides whether an image needs describing?
optionA: How large the image is
optionB: How many images the page contains
optionC: Whether it carries information the reader would otherwise lose
optionD: Whether the image loads quickly
correctAnswerText: Whether it carries information the reader would otherwise lose
explanation: The test is what would be missing without it. Size and quantity have nothing to do with it.

prompt: A team adds a description to every image on the page, including forty decorative dividers. What is the consequence for someone hearing the page read aloud?
optionA: Nothing; more description is always better
optionB: Forty meaningless announcements interrupt the content
optionC: The page becomes faster to navigate
optionD: The decorative images are skipped automatically
correctAnswerText: Forty meaningless announcements interrupt the content
explanation: Every description is read out, so describing nothing-in-particular forty times buries the content. Conscientiousness applied without judgement makes the page worse.

prompt: A page uses a genuine button element for an action. Can a keyboard user reach and operate it?
optionA: No; buttons require a mouse
optionB: Only if extra code is added
optionC: Only if the button carries a description
optionD: Yes; a button is reachable and operable by keyboard as it stands
correctAnswerText: Yes; a button is reachable and operable by keyboard as it stands
explanation: Elements that exist to be operated come with keyboard behaviour already. That is the main practical reason to use them.

prompt: A page makes a plain area of the layout clickable by attaching code to it. Can a keyboard user reach it?
optionA: No; a plain area is not something the keyboard stops at
optionB: Yes; anything clickable is keyboard reachable
optionC: Yes, if it is styled to look like a button
optionD: Only on a page with no other controls
correctAnswerText: No; a plain area is not something the keyboard stops at
explanation: Attaching a click handler adds mouse behaviour and nothing else. The element remains ordinary layout as far as the keyboard is concerned.

prompt: What makes a control reachable by keyboard?
optionA: Being visible on the page
optionB: Being styled to look interactive
optionC: Being the kind of element the keyboard stops at, or being explicitly made one
optionD: Having a click handler attached
correctAnswerText: Being the kind of element the keyboard stops at, or being explicitly made one
explanation: Reachability follows from what the element is rather than how it looks or what code it carries. Styling and handlers are both invisible to keyboard navigation.

prompt: A developer styles a plain area to look exactly like the page other buttons and attaches a click handler. A reviewer using a mouse finds no difference between it and the real buttons. What has the review missed?
optionA: That it is styled differently from the real buttons
optionB: That the keyboard never stops at it, which a mouse review cannot reveal
optionC: That the click handler is slower than a real button
optionD: Nothing; it is equivalent to a real button
correctAnswerText: That the keyboard never stops at it, which a mouse review cannot reveal
explanation: A mouse review exercises the one route that works. The fault is invisible until somebody tries to reach the control another way.

prompt: A page uses heading levels one, two, two, three, two. What does that sequence describe?
optionA: Five sections of equal importance
optionB: A section with four subsections
optionC: Nothing; the sequence is invalid
optionD: A top-level section with three subsections, the first of which has a subsection of its own
correctAnswerText: A top-level section with three subsections, the first of which has a subsection of its own
explanation: Levels state nesting, so each level two opens a subsection of the level one and the level three sits inside the first of them. The sequence is entirely well formed.

prompt: A page uses heading levels one, four, two. What is the problem with jumping from one to four?
optionA: It claims two intervening levels of nesting that do not exist, so the structure is misleading
optionB: Nothing; heading levels may be used in any order
optionC: The page will not display correctly
optionD: Level four headings are not permitted on a page
correctAnswerText: It claims two intervening levels of nesting that do not exist, so the structure is misleading
explanation: Someone navigating by structure is told there are two enclosing levels between them. The page displays perfectly and describes itself wrongly.

prompt: A button shows only a pencil icon and carries no text of any kind. What is announced to somebody hearing the page?
optionA: That there is a pencil icon
optionB: That there is an edit button
optionC: That there is a button, with nothing to say what it does
optionD: Nothing; the button is skipped
correctAnswerText: That there is a button, with nothing to say what it does
explanation: The icon is a picture and conveys nothing to a non-visual reader. The control is reachable and unidentifiable, which is worse than being absent.

prompt: A row of five icon-only buttons carries no text. What does somebody hearing the page encounter?
optionA: Five buttons, distinguishable by their position
optionB: Five buttons, none of which can be told apart
optionC: One button, since the five are identical
optionD: Nothing, since the buttons carry no text
correctAnswerText: Five buttons, none of which can be told apart
explanation: Each is announced as a button and nothing distinguishes them. Guessing which is which by counting positions is not something the page has offered.

prompt: A page contains three controls, appearing in the markup in the order A, B, C, and displayed on screen in that same order. In what order does keyboard focus visit them?
optionA: C, then B, then A
optionB: Whichever is visually closest to the top
optionC: In a random order
optionD: A, then B, then C
correctAnswerText: A, then B, then C
explanation: Focus follows the order in the markup, which here matches the visual order. The two agreeing is what makes ordinary pages behave predictably.

prompt: Three controls appear in the markup in the order A, B, C. Styling places them on screen in the order C, A, B. In what order does keyboard focus visit them?
optionA: A, then B, then C, following the markup rather than the screen
optionB: C, then A, then B, following the screen
optionC: In whichever order they were styled
optionD: Focus visits only the first of the three
correctAnswerText: A, then B, then C, following the markup rather than the screen
explanation: Focus follows the markup and the eye follows the screen, so the two disagree here. A sighted keyboard user watches the focus jump around the page.

prompt: A form is laid out in two visual columns. In the markup, every field of the left column comes first, followed by every field of the right. Focus follows the markup, in which the whole left column precedes the whole right column. A visitor tabbing through expects to move across each row. What do they experience?
optionA: Focus travels across each row as expected
optionB: Focus visits the left column only
optionC: Focus travels down the whole left column before returning to the top of the right
optionD: Focus travels down the right column first
correctAnswerText: Focus travels down the whole left column before returning to the top of the right
explanation: The visual arrangement suggests rows and the markup describes columns. Reordering the markup, rather than restyling, is what aligns the two.

prompt: A table marks overdue rows in red and current rows in green, with no other difference between them. What information is lost to someone who cannot distinguish those colours?
optionA: The contents of the rows
optionB: Which rows are overdue
optionC: The order of the rows
optionD: Nothing at all
correctAnswerText: Which rows are overdue
explanation: The colour is the only carrier of the status, so the status is what disappears. Everything else in the row is still readable.

prompt: A table marks overdue rows in red and also labels each one "Overdue" in a status column. Is this a fault?
optionA: Yes; colour should never be used to convey status
optionB: Yes; the label duplicates the colour unnecessarily
optionC: Only if the red is too pale
optionD: No; the colour is redundant and the information is carried in text as well
correctAnswerText: No; the colour is redundant and the information is carried in text as well
explanation: Colour used alongside another signal is a help rather than a barrier. Removing it would make the table harder for sighted readers and easier for nobody.

prompt: A form marks fields with errors by turning their borders red, and adds no other indication. A visitor reports submitting repeatedly without knowing what was wrong. The red border is the only indication of which fields are at fault and it is a purely visual one. What is the fault?
optionA: The error is conveyed by colour alone, so anyone not perceiving it has nothing to go on
optionB: The red is not bright enough to notice
optionC: The form should not have refused the submission
optionD: The fields should have been marked before submission
correctAnswerText: The error is conveyed by colour alone, so anyone not perceiving it has nothing to go on
explanation: The visitor is told something is wrong and never which field or why. A message associated with each faulty field carries the information regardless of colour.

prompt: A page contains six links, each reading "click here". Read out on their own, what do they convey?
optionA: Their destinations, from the surrounding sentences
optionB: That they are all the same link
optionC: Nothing about where any of them goes
optionD: That the page has six sections
correctAnswerText: Nothing about where any of them goes
explanation: Listing links is a common way of navigating, and six identical entries distinguish nothing. The surrounding sentence is not part of the link.

prompt: Which link text works when read on its own, away from its sentence?
optionA: "Read more"
optionB: "Download the 2024 annual report"
optionC: "Here"
optionD: "This document"
correctAnswerText: "Download the 2024 annual report"
explanation: Only the first names its destination without help. The other three depend entirely on text that does not travel with them.

prompt: A results table gives every row a link reading "View". A team argues the row makes the destination obvious. A list of the links on the page shows the link text without the row it sat in. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The word View is too short to be a link
optionB: The links should open in a new window
optionC: Nothing; the row supplies the context
optionD: Listed on their own, every link reads identically and none can be told from another
correctAnswerText: Listed on their own, every link reads identically and none can be told from another
explanation: Within the row the meaning is clear and the row is exactly what is lost. Naming the subject in each link, visibly or otherwise, is what makes the list usable.

prompt: A form shows an error message in small text at the top of the page after a failed submission. A visitor hearing the page is left at the submit button. What is the difficulty?
optionA: Nothing draws their attention to the message, which is now far from where they are
optionB: The message is too small to read
optionC: The message should be at the bottom instead
optionD: Nothing; the message is on the page
correctAnswerText: Nothing draws their attention to the message, which is now far from where they are
explanation: Being present on the page and being noticed are different things. Somebody reading sequentially has no reason to go back up.

prompt: A form marks a faulty field with a message placed immediately beside it, associated with the field. What does a visitor hearing the page get when they reach that field?
optionA: The field and its name only
optionB: The message only
optionC: The field, its name and the message describing what is wrong
optionD: Nothing, since messages are visual
correctAnswerText: The field, its name and the message describing what is wrong
explanation: Associating the message with the field makes it part of what the field announces. Placement beside it is what helps a sighted reader.

prompt: A form reports errors by scrolling to the first faulty field and turning its border red, without moving keyboard focus or announcing anything. A visitor hearing the page and navigating by keyboard is not moved and is told nothing. What do they experience?
optionA: A clear indication of which field is wrong
optionB: A submission that appears to do nothing at all
optionC: A message read out automatically
optionD: The form being submitted successfully
correctAnswerText: A submission that appears to do nothing at all
explanation: The page changed in ways that reach only a sighted mouse user. Moving focus to the faulty field would carry both the location and its message.

prompt: A company logo appears in the page header as decoration beside the company name in text. How should it be treated?
optionA: Described as the company logo
optionB: Described with the company name
optionC: Described as a decorative image
optionD: Passed over silently, since the name is already present as text
correctAnswerText: Passed over silently, since the name is already present as text
explanation: Describing it would announce the company name twice in succession. The text beside it already carries the information.

prompt: The same company logo is the entire content of a link to the home page, with no text beside it. How should it be treated now?
optionA: Described by where the link goes, since it is the only content the link has
optionB: Passed over silently, as before
optionC: Described as the company logo
optionD: Described as a decorative image
correctAnswerText: Described by where the link goes, since it is the only content the link has
explanation: The image is now carrying the name of a control rather than decorating one. A silently passed over image would leave the link announcing nothing.

prompt: A magnifying-glass icon is the whole content of a button that runs a search. A team describes it as "magnifying glass". The icon is the only content of the button, and what a user needs to know is what pressing it does. What should it be described as?
optionA: A magnifying glass, since that is what the image shows
optionB: A search icon, since that names the image accurately
optionC: What the button does, since the description is naming a control rather than a picture
optionD: Nothing, since icons are decorative
correctAnswerText: What the button does, since the description is naming a control rather than a picture
explanation: Describing the picture tells the user what they cannot see and not what they can do. When an image is a control, its description is the control name.

prompt: A control works perfectly with a mouse and cannot be reached by keyboard at all. It is built from a plain layout element with a click handler. What is the cause?
optionA: The click handler is written incorrectly
optionB: The element is not a kind the keyboard stops at
optionC: The control is styled to hide it from the keyboard
optionD: The browser does not support keyboard navigation
correctAnswerText: The element is not a kind the keyboard stops at
explanation: A click handler adds one route and creates none for the keyboard. Using a real button, or explicitly making the element focusable and operable, is the repair.

prompt: A menu opens on hover and closes as soon as the pointer leaves it. A keyboard user cannot open it at all. The menu opens only in response to a pointer hovering, and a keyboard produces no hover. What is the cause?
optionA: The menu items are not focusable
optionB: The menu closes too quickly to use
optionC: The menu is positioned outside the page
optionD: Opening is tied to an interaction the keyboard cannot produce
correctAnswerText: Opening is tied to an interaction the keyboard cannot produce
explanation: Even perfectly focusable items are unreachable inside a menu that never opens. Opening on focus as well as on hover is what makes both routes work.

prompt: A developer uses a heading element for a line of bold text that is not a heading, because it produced the right size. What does the page now claim?
optionA: That a new section begins there, which is untrue
optionB: Nothing; the size is all that changed
optionC: That the text is important
optionD: That the text should be read first
correctAnswerText: That a new section begins there, which is untrue
explanation: Choosing an element for its appearance puts a false statement into the structure. Anyone navigating by heading is offered a section that does not exist.

prompt: A page lays out a set of related items using a table, because the columns line up neatly. The items have no row-and-column relationship. A table states that its cells are related by row and column, and these items have no such relationship. What does the page claim?
optionA: Nothing; a table is a layout choice
optionB: That the items are in a particular order
optionC: That the items stand in a row-and-column relationship they do not have
optionD: That the items are of equal importance
correctAnswerText: That the items stand in a row-and-column relationship they do not have
explanation: Somebody navigating a table is told which column and row each cell belongs to, and the answers are meaningless here. Layout that carries no relationship should not use an element that asserts one.

prompt: A page presents a chart visually and the same figures in a table below it. Is a reader who cannot see the chart at a disadvantage in what they can learn?
optionA: Yes; they cannot see the chart
optionB: No; the figures are available to both, though the experience differs
optionC: Yes; a table is harder to read than a chart
optionD: No; the two experiences are identical
correctAnswerText: No; the figures are available to both, though the experience differs
explanation: Equivalence is about what can be learned rather than about having the same experience. Both readers can obtain every figure.

prompt: A page offers a phone number for anyone who cannot use its booking form. A team calls this equivalent access. Using the phone route requires another person to act, and the form does not. Is it equivalent?
optionA: Yes; both routes result in a booking
optionB: Yes, provided the phone line is always staffed
optionC: No; a phone number is never an acceptable alternative
optionD: No; one route requires another person and the other does not
correctAnswerText: No; one route requires another person and the other does not
explanation: A route that depends on somebody else answering is not the same as one the person completes themselves. It is a genuine fallback and not equivalence.

prompt: A team builds a separate simplified version of the site for people using screen readers. It carries the same content and is updated less often than the main site. The two versions carry the same content today, and only one of them is updated regularly. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The two will diverge, and the people on the simplified version will silently get older information
optionB: Nothing; a separate version is a reasonable solution
optionC: The simplified version will be too slow
optionD: Screen reader users prefer the main site
correctAnswerText: The two will diverge, and the people on the simplified version will silently get older information
explanation: Equivalence today is not equivalence next month, and the divergence is invisible to the people affected by it. One site that works for everybody has no such drift.

prompt: A video carries captions and no transcript. A team asks whether that is sufficient. Captions appear synchronised with the video and cannot be searched or read at the reader own pace. Who is still not served?
optionA: Nobody; captions cover the requirement
optionB: Only people who cannot hear
optionC: Anyone who cannot hear and cannot see, and anyone wanting to search or skim the content
optionD: Only people on slow connections
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot hear and cannot see, and anyone wanting to search or skim the content
explanation: Captions serve people who can see and not hear, which is a real and partial win. A transcript reaches people using braille output and everyone who would rather read than watch.

prompt: A page is fully operable by keyboard, and reaching the main content requires tabbing through sixty navigation links on every page. A keyboard user passes sixty controls before reaching the content, and a mouse user passes none. Is the page equivalent?
optionA: Yes; everything is reachable by keyboard
optionB: Not in practice; the same information is reachable at a cost nobody else pays
optionC: Yes, since sixty links is not many
optionD: No; the page is not operable by keyboard at all
correctAnswerText: Not in practice; the same information is reachable at a cost nobody else pays
explanation: Reachability is satisfied and the cost is not shared. A link that jumps straight to the main content removes the difference at almost no expense.

prompt: A control cannot be reached by keyboard because it is built from a plain layout element. Four changes are proposed. The barrier is that the keyboard never stops at the element, and only a change to what the element is can alter that. Which removes the barrier?
optionA: Increasing its contrast against the background
optionB: Adding a description to it
optionC: Making it larger and easier to click
optionD: Replacing it with a real button element
correctAnswerText: Replacing it with a real button element
explanation: All four are genuine improvements and three of them address different barriers. Only changing what the element is affects whether the keyboard stops there.

prompt: Status is conveyed by row colour alone. A team proposes darkening the colours so they are easier to distinguish. Darkening changes which colours are used and leaves colour as the only carrier of the status. Does that remove the barrier?
optionA: No; the information is still carried by colour alone
optionB: Yes; the colours will now be distinguishable
optionC: Yes, provided the contrast is checked
optionD: No; the rows should be reordered instead
correctAnswerText: No; the information is still carried by colour alone
explanation: Improving contrast helps people with low vision and is worth doing. It does nothing for somebody who cannot distinguish hues, or for anyone hearing the page.

prompt: A page has a barrier for keyboard users. A team proposes hiding the affected control from screen readers so that it is not announced. Hiding the control removes the announcement and leaves the control unreachable by keyboard. What does that achieve?
optionA: It removes the barrier for both groups
optionB: It removes the barrier for screen reader users only
optionC: It hides the symptom from one group and removes the function from another
optionD: Nothing at all; the page is unchanged
correctAnswerText: It hides the symptom from one group and removes the function from another
explanation: Hiding something that does not work is a way of removing the evidence rather than the fault. Keyboard users are still unable to reach it and now nobody is told it exists.

prompt: A team can fix a barrier affecting a small number of users at significant cost, or fix three smaller barriers affecting many users at the same cost. The single barrier prevents its users from completing the task at all, while the three make the task slower. One group cannot complete the task and the other is merely slowed. What should decide?
optionA: The number of users affected, which favours the three
optionB: That one group cannot complete the task at all, which outranks inconvenience to a larger group
optionC: The cost, which is the same either way
optionD: Neither; both should be deferred until cheaper
correctAnswerText: That one group cannot complete the task at all, which outranks inconvenience to a larger group
explanation: Counting affected users treats prevention and inconvenience as the same quantity. Being unable to complete a task is a different kind of harm from taking longer over it.

prompt: An automated checker reports no problems on a page. A team concludes the page is accessible. The checker examines what can be determined from the markup and cannot judge whether a description is meaningful or an order is sensible. What has been established?
optionA: That the page is accessible
optionB: That the page has no barriers for screen reader users
optionC: Nothing; automated checkers are useless
optionD: That the page passes the checks the tool performs, which are a subset of what matters
correctAnswerText: That the page passes the checks the tool performs, which are a subset of what matters
explanation: Automated checking genuinely catches missing descriptions and unlabelled controls, which is worth having. Whether a description says anything useful is not something a tool can decide.

prompt: A ticket machine presents every option on a touchscreen and has no physical buttons. The screen requires the user to see where to touch, and the machine offers no other way to select an option. Who is prevented from using it?
optionA: Anyone who cannot see the screen
optionB: Anyone unfamiliar with ticket machines
optionC: Anyone in a hurry
optionD: Nobody; touchscreens are universally usable
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot see the screen
explanation: The barrier is the same as an unlabelled control on a page, in a machine with no markup at all. A physical keypad or audio guidance is the equivalent remedy.

prompt: A telephone menu system announces its options and requires a response within three seconds. A caller who needs longer to process the options is cut off before choosing. The options are announced once and the response window is fixed at three seconds. What is the barrier?
optionA: The menu has too many options
optionB: The announcements are too quiet
optionC: A fixed time limit that some callers cannot meet, with no way to repeat the options
optionD: Nothing; three seconds is a reasonable time
correctAnswerText: A fixed time limit that some callers cannot meet, with no way to repeat the options
explanation: This is a time limit with no extension, which is a recognised barrier on a page as well. Allowing the options to be repeated, or removing the limit, is the remedy.

prompt: A printed form asks respondents to tick a box in one of two coloured columns, with no other label distinguishing them. A team argues that a printed form is outside the scope of accessibility work. The two columns are distinguished by colour alone and carry no other label. Is the argument sound?
optionA: Yes; accessibility applies to digital products
optionB: No; the barrier is the same one, and being printed does not change who it excludes
optionC: Yes, provided a digital version is also offered
optionD: No; printed forms should not use colour at all
correctAnswerText: No; the barrier is the same one, and being printed does not change who it excludes
explanation: The medium changes the remedy and not the reasoning. A heading on each column removes the barrier as surely as a text label removes it on a page.

prompt: A team must decide whether to build accessibility into a new product from the start or to audit and remedy it before release. Retrofitting has previously required changing the structure of pages rather than their styling. Barriers of this kind live in the structure, and changing structure late is far more expensive than choosing it early. Which fits?
optionA: Auditing before release, since it can be done once for the whole product
optionB: Auditing before release, since the product may change during development
optionC: Either, since the resulting product is the same
optionD: Building it in from the start, since the barriers live in decisions made early
correctAnswerText: Building it in from the start, since the barriers live in decisions made early
explanation: The resulting product can indeed be the same, which is why cost is what decides. Element choices and focus order are structural, and structure is what a late remedy has to unpick.
